# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage
under the module's equivalence tests shows how much of its behaviour they compare, set
against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its
Rust's.

description: "The patterns by which safe Rust over C has reached undefined behaviour in Crustify's campaigns, each with what prevents it and which check catches it, and how the catalogue grows from proven findings. Read before analysing, binding or porting any item, before writing its UB tests, and when reviewing for UB or contracts."

# Soundness patterns

The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a
memory-safety defect of the C that it had to keep out of its safe API. Every pattern here
has a proven finding of a campaign behind it: the catalogue records what went wrong, not
what could. An item's analysis asks of each pattern whether the item can meet it, and a
review for UB or contracts reads the item against the same list, so that a defect one
module met is not met again in the next.

## 1. Patterns

Each pattern has an id, which a finding's report names. What prevents a pattern is stated
as what the Rust does; [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md) and [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md)
give the routes that do it.

### 1.1 Values the C trusts

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unchecked-arithmetic` | The C computes with a value a safe caller controls and does not check it: a signed overflow, a shift, a size that wraps with its header, a zero divisor. | The Rust checks the value's range before the call, sizes past `isize::MAX` included, and refuses what the C would compute wrongly. | UBSan, review |
| `diverging-precheck` | A check in Rust repeats the C's parsing or evaluation and differs from what the C then computes. | The Rust validates the exact value the C will use, or computes the result itself and hands the C only that. | UBSan |
| `degenerate-input` | The C reads out of bounds on an input its own validation accepts, such as an empty string beside others or a null pointer for a string. | Every wrapper that can route the input to that reader refuses or normalises it, the indirect routes included. | ASan |
| `variant-mismatch` | A tagged, variable-size value of another variant than its container expects is passed on, and the C sizes its buffers by the container's. | The Rust compares the value's variant with the container's before any call that looks it up or formats it. | ASan |

### 1.2 Memory and ownership

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `size-known-to-c` | Only the C knows an object's true size or layout: an opaque type, a pointer a tag types, a base struct its callbacks read past, an array sized by a count. Rust builds it too small or types it wrongly. | Such an object is allocated through the C alone, a tagged pointer is typed only where its tag is vouched for, and an object whose callbacks read more than Rust built is refused. | ASan, review |
| `hidden-dependency` | A handle, a lent pointer or a callback outlives something it depends on without showing it: a parent it points back to, a global the program may close, lent memory the C copied into a second slot. | The handle's lifetime is tied to that owner, or it keeps the owner alive; a pointer the C stores is bounded by its longest-lived reader. | ASan, Miri, review |
| `failure-leaves-state` | A failure path of the C, most often a failed allocation, leaves an object uninitialised, freed, wrongly sized or half written and still returns, sometimes reporting success. | The Rust trusts nothing the C leaves after a failure: it validates outputs again, does not reuse the object, and composes the operation itself where the C's error path is unsafe. | ASan, UBSan, review |
| `allocator-rule` | The binding vouches for a rule of alignment or allocation that some build or allocator of the C does not keep: the maximum alignment, a zero-size resize, who may free whose storage. | It vouches only for what every configured allocator guarantees, and checks alignment at each constructor that copies. | Miri, UBSan, review |
| `adoption-condition` | An adoption takes ownership without stating when the C owns the storage: a sentinel pointer at zero capacity, one element listed twice, a buffer a pool still tracks. | The contract states the exact condition, and the Rust checks it before the owner can free or resize. | ASan, review |
| `count-wrap` | A reference count the C does not check wraps once safe Rust can leak clones, and the object is freed early. | A count that can wrap within a process's lifetime is checked before each increment, and the clone fails or aborts before it wraps. | Miri, review |
| `uninitialised-as-data` | Memory the C leaves unwritten is exposed as initialised Rust data, or the argument that the C writes it is false on some path. | The Rust views it as uninitialised until every path of the C is shown to write it; an export takes raw pointers and builds no reference over memory its caller may have left unwritten. | Miri, review |
| `aliasing-at-the-boundary` | A pointer the C keeps is derived from a borrow that a later reborrow ends, or Rust holds a reference over memory the C still writes or shares. | Every pointer the C keeps is derived from the original raw pointer, and a reference is handed out only over a span no C writer or co-owner reaches. | Miri, BSan, review |

### 1.3 Threads and callbacks

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unsynchronised-global` | The C reads and writes global state, or initialises it lazily on first use, without synchronisation, so that safe calls on unrelated objects race. | The Rust initialises or serialises that state before any safe call reaches it. | TSan, review |
| `assumed-locking` | A `Send` or `Sync` proof assumes the C object's own locking covers every access, but a path skips the lock, reads after releasing it, or the object has none. | Thread safety is derived from every reader and writer of each field. | review |
| `callback-state` | A trampoline mishandles a panic, a refusal or a re-entry: a stored panic goes stale or a nested call drops it, a drop panics, the C goes on after a refusal, or the callback runs under a lock of the C. | A stored panic or stop belongs to one outermost call of the C, no drop panics, and a stop is promised only where the C can be stopped. | review |

A `# Safety` contract or a `// SAFETY:` proof that is wrong in a way no pattern above names
is still a finding: a contract is derived again from every safe method that relies on it
whenever one is added.

## 2. Findings

A finding of the `ub` or `contracts` objective names its pattern, or `new`, as
[`reviewing-reports`](../../verification/reviewing/reports/SKILL.md)'s Reports section describes. A
sanitizer's false positive is no finding and names none.

A finding of a known pattern means that its statement did not let the analysis recognise
the case, or that what prevents it was not enough. A finding that is `new` is a pattern the
catalogue lacks.

## 3. Evolution

The catalogue changes only from findings a reproducer proves, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes:

- a `new` finding is proposed as a pattern once it is stated without the target's names,
  with the finding as its evidence; one that can only be stated in the target's names is
  that campaign's lesson;
- a pattern whose findings recur has its statement or its prevention sharpened, from the
  findings that escaped it; and
- a pattern no campaign has met since it was written stays: its absence is what the
  catalogue is for.

What tells whether the catalogue works is the count of findings of known patterns, over
the modules integrated since a pattern was written, taken together: it falls against the
modules before, or the catalogue is not what prevents them. One module alone tells nothing,
since modules differ. The unsafe sites the reviews read, which the count would be taken
against, are not recorded yet. The count of `new` findings tells how much of what goes wrong
the catalogue does not hold yet.

## 6. items[*]

Every field is required on every item, and no other field is accepted.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | C entity name, non-empty: a function pointer written inline is named by its signature |
| `defined_in` | path of its definition below the C root |
| `kind` | what the C entity is: `struct`, `union`, `enum`, `function`, `global`, `macro`, `function_pointer`, declared by a typedef or written inline, or `typedef`, one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer |
| `field_users` | the members of a struct, a union or an enum its consumers use: a struct's or a union's fields, whose accessors the batch writes, or an enum's constants; empty on any other kind |
| `typedefs` | the typedefs that name a struct, a union, an enum or a function pointer besides its `name`, which the batch binds with it; empty on any other kind |
| `home` | `.rs` path, relative to the repository's root, the item is authored into |

`(name, defined_in)` identifies an item and must be unique within the batch. A
`port/layout` batch holds only structs, unions and enums, a `port/memory` batch only
structs and unions, and a `port/unexport` batch only functions, globals and function
pointers.
`field_users` and `typedefs` must not repeat a name.

`home` is the sole placement input: no other artifact decides where an item goes, so the
Rust tree a wave's batches name is not restructured while the wave runs.

## 7. Routes

`kind` selects the agent route, and every item in a batch must select the same one. A
batch mixing routes is rejected.

| kind | route |
|---|---|
| `struct`, `union`, `enum`, `typedef`, and a `macro` that generates types | `type` |
| `function`, `global`, `function_pointer`, and any other `macro` | `symbol` |

A macro generates types when its record in the planning tools lists the instance types it
mints: its instances share the one generic the type route writes for it, as
[`binding-symbols`](../../rust/binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section describes.

A batch of a foundational module routes like any other. Its `module` and `foundational`
name the module, which `modules.json` marks `foundational`, and its items with a lifecycle
role are bound as strategies (`binding-symbols`, Lifecycle strategies).

content.content:
---
name: bindgen
description: "How the raw bindings are laid out, generated, built in each mode, landed and published. Read before changing allowlists, shims, wrapper headers or build.rs, or scaffolding the bindings."
---

# Raw bindings

How a campaign's raw bindings are laid out, generated, built and shipped. They are
generated by bindgen from the C under `c/`, one module per link unit, and ship inside the
safe crate as its public `sys` module, with the C they bind: the published crate carries
the generated bindings, so that a dependent builds without bindgen or libclang, and the C
that remains, so that a dependent has the whole library and reaches what is not
translated yet through the raw bindings. How the safe crate uses them is
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s; their lints and formatting are
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Generated code section's.

## 1. Layout

```text
<repository>/
├── Cargo.toml            the safe crate's manifest; bindgen an optional build dependency
├── build.rs              builds or locates the C, compiles the C wrappers, regenerates on request
├── c/                    the C that remains, built into the crate
├── sys/<link-unit>/      one link unit's bindings
│   ├── wrapper.h         the headers they cover: the installed headers, and the internal headers its batches bind items of
│   ├── allowlist.txt     one `function|type|var <regex>` per line, filled by the batches
│   ├── external.txt      the types other link units' bindings own, one regex per line
│   ├── shims.h
│   ├── shims.c           the `crustify_<NAME>` macro shims
│   ├── bindings.rs       generated, committed
│   └── static_fns.c      generated wrappers of the allowlisted `static inline` functions, committed
└── src/sys.rs            the `sys` module: one public module per link unit, including its committed or regenerated bindings, or their doctest copy, and the re-exports of the types other link units own
```

Everything a build reads sits inside the crate, so that the packaged crate builds on its
own: no path leaves it, and `crustify/` is read only in campaign mode.

Within a link unit's Rust, `crate::sys::<link_unit>` is imported as `sys`, so that a raw
binding is `sys::<name>`, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming section spells it.
The `sys` module is public: a consumer reaches the C that is not translated yet through
it, under its C names. It takes the place of the ecosystem's `-sys` crates, and is named after them.

`c/` is the C that remains: in a wrap campaign the whole source, and in a port campaign
the fork's `main`, which each switch trims of the module it ports, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes. A build of
the crate therefore never holds both a module's C and the Rust that replaces it: the
remaining C reaches a ported module through the safe crate's exports, under their bare C
names, as the conventions' Exports section describes.

## 2. Generation

The bindings follow from the headers at the `c/` revision, the allowlists, the generator
settings below, the bindgen version, pinned exactly in `Cargo.toml`, and the LLVM pinned
below, so that generating
twice from the same input gives the same bytes. The settings are the same for every
campaign:

- the output is formatted by bindgen's own formatter (`prettyplease`), never by the
  toolchain's `rustfmt`, whose output differs between toolchains, so that a nightly build
  regenerates the bytes a stable one committed;
- enums are generated as constants (`Consts`), without the enum name as a prefix, which
  the safe types that bind them convert, as [`binding-types`](../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Enums
  section describes;
- `Default` is derived, and layout tests are generated;
- C comments are kept as doc comments, and no doctest is collected from them, since they
  hold C: the generated modules are modules of the safe crate, which rustdoc cannot exempt
  one by one, so its doctests are collected from a copy of whichever bindings the build
  uses, committed or regenerated, whose C comments are plain comments: the build script
  writes it into `OUT_DIR`, and `src/sys.rs` includes it in their place under
  `cfg(doctest)`;
- each allowlisted `static inline` function gets a compiled wrapper, `<name>__extern`, in
  `static_fns.c`, and is bound under its own name through
  `#[link_name = "<name>__extern"]`, so that it is called as an exported function is:
  bindgen's `wrap_static_fns`;
- macro shims are bound like the functions they wrap; and
- an empty allowlist generates no item: `bindings.rs` holds only bindgen's banner, and
  `static_fns.c` stays, empty, so that every link unit has both generated files.

An internal header's declarations are generated, and the wrappers of its `static inline`
functions compiled, as the link unit's own translation units see them: with the include
dirs and preprocessor definitions the build of the C a mode links records for them, its
generated headers and its out-of-tree libraries' include dirs among them, and the source
dirs taken from the checkout's `c/`. An item whose declaration depends on a definition that
differs between the variants is generated from the `plain` variant's configuration in every
mode, so that the committed bindings are those of every variant.

A type that another link unit's bindings own is blocklisted, as `external.txt` lists it,
and re-exported from that link unit's module under its C name, so that each C type has one
Rust type across the crate. A type an out-of-tree library's wrapper publishes is
re-exported as its wrapper's safe type, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes.

The bindings are generated for the campaign's target, the host's, as the setup workflow's
Builds section names it, the only target the crate supports: `src/sys.rs` fails to compile
on any other, naming it.

The C an out-of-tree library's wrapper bundles once its side campaign has ported part of
the library is compiled with its symbols prefixed, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Side campaigns section asks:
a generated header, force-included in every compile of that C and of its shims and
wrappers, renames each global symbol the library defines to `crustify_<library>_<name>`,
and bindgen binds each item under its C name with the prefixed symbol as its `link_name`,
so that the Rust names stay C's. The crate passes the header's path to the C builds of the
crates that depend on it through its build script's metadata, under its `links` key, and
those force-include it too, so that their C calls the same copy.

# Raw bindings

How a campaign's raw bindings are laid out, generated, built and shipped. They are
generated by bindgen from the C under `c/`, one module per link unit, and ship inside the
safe crate as its public `sys` module, with the C they bind: the published crate carries
the generated bindings, so that a dependent builds without bindgen or libclang, and the C
that remains, so that a dependent has the whole library and reaches what is not
translated yet through the raw bindings. How the safe crate uses them is
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s; their lints and formatting are
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Generated code section's.

## 1. Layout

```text
<repository>/
├── Cargo.toml            the safe crate's manifest; bindgen an optional build dependency
├── build.rs              builds or locates the C, compiles the C wrappers, regenerates on request
├── c/                    the C that remains, built into the crate
├── sys/<link-unit>/      one link unit's bindings
│   ├── wrapper.h         the headers they cover: the installed headers, and the internal headers its batches bind items of
│   ├── allowlist.txt     one `function|type|var <regex>` per line, filled by the batches
│   ├── external.txt      the types other link units' bindings own, one regex per line
│   ├── shims.h
│   ├── shims.c           the `crustify_<NAME>` macro shims
│   ├── bindings.rs       generated, committed
│   └── static_fns.c      generated wrappers of the allowlisted `static inline` functions, committed
└── src/sys.rs            the `sys` module: one public module per link unit, including its committed or regenerated bindings, or their doctest copy, and the re-exports of the types other link units own
```

Everything a build reads sits inside the crate, so that the packaged crate builds on its
own: no path leaves it, and `crustify/` is read only in campaign mode.

Within a link unit's Rust, `crate::sys::<link_unit>` is imported as `sys`, so that a raw
binding is `sys::<name>`, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming section spells it.
The `sys` module is public: a consumer reaches the C that is not translated yet through
it, under its C names. It takes the place of the ecosystem's `-sys` crates, and is named after them.

`c/` is the C that remains: in a wrap campaign the whole source, and in a port campaign
the fork's `main`, which each switch trims of the module it ports, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes. A build of
the crate therefore never holds both a module's C and the Rust that replaces it: the
remaining C reaches a ported module through the safe crate's exports, under their bare C
names, as the conventions' Exports section describes.

## 2. Generation

The bindings follow from the headers at the `c/` revision, the allowlists, the generator
settings below, the bindgen version, pinned exactly in `Cargo.toml`, and the LLVM pinned
below, so that generating
twice from the same input gives the same bytes. The settings are the same for every
campaign:

- the output is formatted by bindgen's own formatter (`prettyplease`), never by the
  toolchain's `rustfmt`, whose output differs between toolchains, so that a nightly build
  regenerates the bytes a stable one committed;
- enums are generated as constants (`Consts`), without the enum name as a prefix, which
  the safe types that bind them convert, as [`binding-types`](../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Enums
  section describes;
- `Default` is derived, and layout tests are generated;
- C comments are kept as doc comments, and no doctest is collected from them, since they
  hold C: the generated modules are modules of the safe crate, which rustdoc cannot exempt
  one by one, so its doctests are collected from a copy of whichever bindings the build
  uses, committed or regenerated, whose C comments are plain comments: the build script
  writes it into `OUT_DIR`, and `src/sys.rs` includes it in their place under
  `cfg(doctest)`;
- each allowlisted `static inline` function gets a compiled wrapper, `<name>__extern`, in
  `static_fns.c`, and is bound under its own name through
  `#[link_name = "<name>__extern"]`, so that it is called as an exported function is:
  bindgen's `wrap_static_fns`;
- macro shims are bound like the functions they wrap; and
- an empty allowlist generates no item: `bindings.rs` holds only bindgen's banner, and
  `static_fns.c` stays, empty, so that every link unit has both generated files.

An internal header's declarations are generated, and the wrappers of its `static inline`
functions compiled, as the link unit's own translation units see them: with the include
dirs and preprocessor definitions the build of the C a mode links records for them, its
generated headers and its out-of-tree libraries' include dirs among them, and the source
dirs taken from the checkout's `c/`. An item whose declaration depends on a definition that
differs between the variants is generated from the `plain` variant's configuration in every
mode, so that the committed bindings are those of every variant.

A type that another link unit's bindings own is blocklisted, as `external.txt` lists it,
and re-exported from that link unit's module under its C name, so that each C type has one
Rust type across the crate. A type an out-of-tree library's wrapper publishes is
re-exported as its wrapper's safe type, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes.

The bindings are generated for the campaign's target, the host's, as the setup workflow's

on any other, naming it.

The C an out-of-tree library's wrapper bundles once its side campaign has ported part of
the library is compiled with its symbols prefixed, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Side campaigns section asks:

wrappers, renames each global symbol the library defines to `crustify_<library>_<name>`,

crates that depend on it through its build script's metadata, under its `links` key, and
those force-include it too, so that their C calls the same copy.

system include dirs, is pinned with the bindgen version: its install prefix and version, in
the workspace manifest's `[workspace.metadata.crustify]`, as `bindgen-llvm` and

another libclang of its own, and fails, naming both versions, when the pinned one is
missing or reports another version. A dependent's regeneration into `OUT_DIR`, compared
with nothing, takes the LLVM its host finds.

## 3. Build modes

The build script runs in one of four modes:

| mode | when | C |

# Rust

How the Rust a campaign generates is built, linted and formatted: its toolchains, its
edition, the lints every crate inherits and how it is formatted. What the code is named and
where it sits is [`conventions`](../conventions/SKILL.md)'s; these are the rules the toolchain
enforces on it.

## 1. Toolchains

The workspace builds and tests on stable Rust, pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml` to the
stable release current when the repository is created, with the `clippy` and `rustfmt`
components. Miri, the sanitizer and coverage instrumentation of the Rust,
BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain aside, and the formatter's unstable options need
nightly: a nightly pinned by date, recorded in the workspace manifest as
`[workspace.metadata.crustify] nightly = "nightly-<date>"`, and named explicitly wherever it
runs. A toolchain is moved forward only between waves, in a
commit of its own.

## 2. Edition and manifests

Every crate uses Rust edition 2024, with the workspace's `rust-version` set to the pinned
stable release. The shared package fields (`edition`, `rust-version`, `license`,
`repository`) are declared once, in `[workspace.package]`, and inherited. Every crate
inherits the workspace's lints with `[lints] workspace = true`.

## 3. Lints

The workspace declares its lints in `[workspace.lints.rust]` and `[workspace.lints.clippy]`.
Every gate runs with warnings denied, so a lint at `warn` fails a landing as surely as one
at `deny`; `deny` marks the lints no item may opt out of.

### 3.1 rustc

| lint | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `nonstandard_style` (`non_snake_case`, `non_camel_case_types`, `non_upper_case_globals`) | `deny` | the naming the conventions' Naming section gives: `snake_case` functions, methods, modules and variables, `UpperCamelCase` types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` constants and statics |
| `unsafe_code` | `warn` | unsafe code only in a module's unsafe regions, which take it back, as [Unsafe code](#5-unsafe-code) describes |
| `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` | `deny` | each unsafe operation in an `unsafe fn` sits in its own justified `unsafe` block |
| `missing_docs` | `warn` | every public item carries its anchor, which is a doc comment |
| `rust_2018_idioms` | `warn` | elided lifetimes in paths and other pre-2018 idioms |
| `unreachable_pub`, `unused_qualifications`, `unused_lifetimes`, `let_underscore_drop`, `trivial_casts`, `trivial_numeric_casts` | `warn` | visibility the crate does not need, and casts and drops that hide intent at the foreign boundary |

### 3.2 Clippy

| lints | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::correctness` | `deny` | code that is outright wrong |
| `clippy::all` (`suspicious`, `style`, `complexity`, `perf`), `clippy::pedantic`, `clippy::cargo` | `warn` | as much of Clippy's stable guidance as applies; `nursery` is left out, its lints still being unsettled |
| `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block`, `missing_safety_doc`, `unnecessary_safety_comment`, `unnecessary_safety_doc` | `deny` | every `unsafe` block is one justified operation, and every safety comment and `# Safety` section is where it belongs |
| `mem_forget`, `allow_attributes`, `allow_attributes_without_reason` | `deny` | no leak by `mem::forget`, and every exception an `#[expect]` with a reason |
| `module_inception` | `allow` | a C directory often holds a TU of its own name, so the mirrored tree nests a module in one of its name |
| `module_name_repetitions` | `allow` | items keep their C-derived names where their module, mirrored from the C path, repeats them |
| `multiple_crate_versions` | `allow` | the dependency graph is not the campaign's to dedupe |

An item that needs an exception takes it locally, as
`#[expect(<lint>, reason = "<why>")]`, never as a crate-wide `allow`: the expectation fails
once the exception is no longer needed.

### 3.3 Generated code

The raw bindings' bindgen output follows C's names and shapes, so it is exempt from the
workspace's lints: `src/sys.rs` allows every lint and lint group the workspace sets over
each generated module, under one `#[expect(clippy::allow_attributes, reason = "…")]`
naming the generated code, and the formatter skips the generated modules. The
hand-written parts of the raw bindings, such as `build.rs`, `src/sys.rs` itself and the
macro shims, follow the rest of this spec.

## 4. Formatting

Every crate is formatted by `rustfmt`, configured once in the workspace's `rustfmt.toml`:

| option | value |
|---|---|
| `edition`, `style_edition` | `"2024"` |
| `max_width`, `comment_width` | `100` |
| `newline_style` | `"Unix"` |
| `use_field_init_shorthand`, `use_try_shorthand` | `true` |
| `imports_granularity` | `"Module"` |
| `group_imports` | `"StdExternalCrate"` |
| `wrap_comments`, `normalize_comments`, `normalize_doc_attributes` | `true` |
| `format_code_in_doc_comments`, `format_macro_matchers` | `true` |
| `hex_literal_case` | `"Upper"` |
| `reorder_impl_items` | `true` |

The options from `imports_granularity` down are unstable, so the formatter runs on the
pinned nightly. A landing's tree is formatted, and the gate checks that it is.

## 5. Unsafe code

Every unsafe block carries a specific, falsifiable `// SAFETY:` comment: the invariant the
operation relies on, and why it holds on every path that reaches it. Native Rust APIs are
safe unless their caller obligation cannot be expressed in the type system; an `unsafe fn`
documents that obligation in its `# Safety` section.

Unsafe code sits only in a module's unsafe regions and in the raw bindings, as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes. A region that
holds unsafe code of its own takes `unsafe_code` back where it is declared, as
`#[expect(unsafe_code, reason = "<what it reaches>")] mod ffi_import { … }`, so that the
expectation fails once the region holds none; and so does each test suite and unit-test
module that holds unsafe code. A region whose only unsafe code a macro of another crate
expands takes none: the lint does not see that code, and the expectation would fail. A
module with no region carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, which no item within it can take
back.

1. its link unit's `allowlist.txt` gains only the FFI items its items need, and
   `wrapper.h` an internal header only when one of them is declared there;
2. a shim is added to `shims.h` and `shims.c` only for a macro whose expansion depends on
   the build's configuration, as `crustify_<NAME>`, as
   [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section describes;
3. the bindings are regenerated, in campaign mode with `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` set; and
4. the safe crate is built and tested against them.

Where its link unit's headers name a type another link unit owns, the batch also extends
what the re-export needs, and only that: the type joins its own link unit's `external.txt`,
the owning link unit's `allowlist.txt` too while its bindings lack the type, and the link
unit's module in `src/sys.rs` re-exports it from the owner's, under its C name.

An allowlist or `wrapper.h` change alone leaves the C library as it is, so it reuses a
prebuilt variant; a shim compiles with the crate, as [Build modes](#3-build-modes) describes.

## 5. Landing

A batch that changes an allowlist, `external.txt`, a shim or `wrapper.h` regenerates the
bindings and commits them in the same landing, so that the committed bindings always match
their input. The gates that check it, and that the crate packages, are
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section's.

## 6. Publishing

The safe crate is published with its raw bindings and the C it bundles. The packaged crate
holds the layout above, `src/`, the files of `c/` that the bundled build reads and the
C's license files, and nothing else of the repository but its README and the files the
package manager adds to every package, such as its manifest's original and its lockfile.

# Rust

How the Rust a campaign generates is built, linted and formatted: its toolchains, its
edition, the lints every crate inherits and how it is formatted. What the code is named and
where it sits is [`conventions`](../conventions/SKILL.md)'s; these are the rules the toolchain
enforces on it.

## 1. Toolchains

The workspace builds and tests on stable Rust, pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml` to the
stable release current when the repository is created, with the `clippy` and `rustfmt`
components. Miri, the sanitizer and coverage instrumentation of the Rust,
BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain aside, and the formatter's unstable options need
nightly: a nightly pinned by date, recorded in the workspace manifest as
`[workspace.metadata.crustify] nightly = "nightly-<date>"`, and named explicitly wherever it
runs. A toolchain is moved forward only between waves, in a
commit of its own.

## 2. Edition and manifests

Every crate uses Rust edition 2024, with the workspace's `rust-version` set to the pinned
stable release. The shared package fields (`edition`, `rust-version`, `license`,
`repository`) are declared once, in `[workspace.package]`, and inherited. Every crate
inherits the workspace's lints with `[lints] workspace = true`.

## 3. Lints

The workspace declares its lints in `[workspace.lints.rust]` and `[workspace.lints.clippy]`.
Every gate runs with warnings denied, so a lint at `warn` fails a landing as surely as one
at `deny`; `deny` marks the lints no item may opt out of.

### 3.1 rustc

| lint | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `nonstandard_style` (`non_snake_case`, `non_camel_case_types`, `non_upper_case_globals`) | `deny` | the naming the conventions' Naming section gives: `snake_case` functions, methods, modules and variables, `UpperCamelCase` types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` constants and statics |
| `unsafe_code` | `warn` | unsafe code only in a module's unsafe regions, which take it back, as [Unsafe code](#5-unsafe-code) describes |
| `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` | `deny` | each unsafe operation in an `unsafe fn` sits in its own justified `unsafe` block |
| `missing_docs` | `warn` | every public item carries its anchor, which is a doc comment |
| `rust_2018_idioms` | `warn` | elided lifetimes in paths and other pre-2018 idioms |
| `unreachable_pub`, `unused_qualifications`, `unused_lifetimes`, `let_underscore_drop`, `trivial_casts`, `trivial_numeric_casts` | `warn` | visibility the crate does not need, and casts and drops that hide intent at the foreign boundary |

### 3.2 Clippy

| lints | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::correctness` | `deny` | code that is outright wrong |
| `clippy::all` (`suspicious`, `style`, `complexity`, `perf`), `clippy::pedantic`, `clippy::cargo` | `warn` | as much of Clippy's stable guidance as applies; `nursery` is left out, its lints still being unsettled |
| `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block`, `missing_safety_doc`, `unnecessary_safety_comment`, `unnecessary_safety_doc` | `deny` | every `unsafe` block is one justified operation, and every safety comment and `# Safety` section is where it belongs |
| `mem_forget`, `allow_attributes`, `allow_attributes_without_reason` | `deny` | no leak by `mem::forget`, and every exception an `#[expect]` with a reason |
| `module_inception` | `allow` | a C directory often holds a TU of its own name, so the mirrored tree nests a module in one of its name |
| `module_name_repetitions` | `allow` | items keep their C-derived names where their module, mirrored from the C path, repeats them |
| `multiple_crate_versions` | `allow` | the dependency graph is not the campaign's to dedupe |

An item that needs an exception takes it locally, as
`#[expect(<lint>, reason = "<why>")]`, never as a crate-wide `allow`: the expectation fails
once the exception is no longer needed.

### 3.3 Generated code

The raw bindings' bindgen output follows C's names and shapes, so it is exempt from the
workspace's lints: `src/sys.rs` allows every lint and lint group the workspace sets over
each generated module, under one `#[expect(clippy::allow_attributes, reason = "…")]`
naming the generated code, and the formatter skips the generated modules. The
hand-written parts of the raw bindings, such as `build.rs`, `src/sys.rs` itself and the
macro shims, follow the rest of this spec.

## 4. Formatting

Every crate is formatted by `rustfmt`, configured once in the workspace's `rustfmt.toml`:

| option | value |
|---|---|
| `edition`, `style_edition` | `"2024"` |
| `max_width`, `comment_width` | `100` |
| `newline_style` | `"Unix"` |
| `use_field_init_shorthand`, `use_try_shorthand` | `true` |
| `imports_granularity` | `"Module"` |
| `group_imports` | `"StdExternalCrate"` |
| `wrap_comments`, `normalize_comments`, `normalize_doc_attributes` | `true` |
| `format_code_in_doc_comments`, `format_macro_matchers` | `true` |
| `hex_literal_case` | `"Upper"` |
| `reorder_impl_items` | `true` |

The options from `imports_granularity` down are unstable, so the formatter runs on the
pinned nightly. A landing's tree is formatted, and the gate checks that it is.

## 5. Unsafe code

Every unsafe block carries a specific, falsifiable `// SAFETY:` comment: the invariant the
operation relies on, and why it holds on every path that reaches it. Native Rust APIs are
safe unless their caller obligation cannot be expressed in the type system; an `unsafe fn`
documents that obligation in its `# Safety` section.

Unsafe code sits only in a module's unsafe regions and in the raw bindings, as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes. A region that
holds unsafe code of its own takes `unsafe_code` back where it is declared, as
`#[expect(unsafe_code, reason = "<what it reaches>")] mod ffi_import { … }`, so that the
expectation fails once the region holds none; and so does each test suite and unit-test
module that holds unsafe code. A region whose only unsafe code a macro of another crate
expands takes none: the lint does not see that code, and the expectation would fail. A
module with no region carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, which no item within it can take
back.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

## Legend

- `module` / `wave` / `batch` — the batch's place in `schedule.json`: its wave's module and
  the wave and batch indices
- `objective` — `wrap` or `port`; `pass` — `first` for a translation batch, `review` for a
  review batch; `Σ first` / `Σ review` total each pass apart
- `types` / `symbols` / `fields` — the batch's scheduled units (callbacks count as
  symbols) and its types' assigned field accessors; a review row counts what it reviewed
- `$` / `tokens` / `wall` — the agent's computed cost (API-equivalent under
  subscription), its tokens in millions as `crustify usage` reports them, and its elapsed
  time, C rebuild included; `$/<unit>` divides `$` by the row's units
- `+LoC` — the landing's Rust insertions/deletions; `loc` — its `.rs` insertions
- `cov (C/Rust)` — line coverage after the landing, all test workloads in one run: C over
  the link unit's TUs, Rust over non-test sources; a `Σ` cell is the pass's last landing
- `+UB safe tests` … `+unit tests` — the tests the landing added, with its C/Rust coverage
  change in pp
- `+lifecycle` … `+misc`, `total` — the reports a review batch filed, by kind
- safety audit columns — the Safety audit's metrics, as a landing changed them
- API stability columns — the landing's items by how `ffimap api` classifies their consumer-facing API against its base: `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed`, `new`, and `→Replaces` for the anchors a port moved; `unattributed` the crate's public items no anchor reaches, by module; `reasons` the changed and removed items with the reason the batch recorded
- `cost` / `review cost` / `total` — a module's translation, review and combined cost;
  `module wall` — first launch to final gate; `Σ recorded agents` leaves the assistant
  out, `Σ campaign` adds it, without per-unit cells
- `UB safe tests` … `Unit tests` — `#[test]` functions per suite, each with the coverage of
  running it alone; `Total tests` — all four, whose coverage is one joint run's union,
  never the sum
- `total`, `ported` and `wrapped` types and symbols — the scheduled public-API units, and
  those with a `Replaces:` or a `Wraps:` anchor at the tip; `share` is of the total

## Legend

- `module` / `wave` / `batch` — the batch's place in `schedule.json`: its wave's module and
  the wave and batch indices
- `objective` — `wrap` or `port`; `pass` — `first` for a translation batch, `review` for a
  review batch; `Σ first` / `Σ review` total each pass apart
- `types` / `symbols` / `fields` — the batch's scheduled units (callbacks count as
  symbols) and its types' assigned field accessors; a review row counts what it reviewed
- `$` / `tokens` / `wall` — the agent's computed cost (API-equivalent under
  subscription), its tokens in millions as `crustify usage` reports them, and its elapsed
  time, C rebuild included; `$/<unit>` divides `$` by the row's units
- `+LoC` — the landing's Rust insertions/deletions; `loc` — its `.rs` insertions
- `cov (C/Rust)` — line coverage after the landing, all test workloads in one run: C over
  the link unit's TUs, Rust over non-test sources; a `Σ` cell is the pass's last landing
- `+UB safe tests` … `+unit tests` — the tests the landing added, with its C/Rust coverage
  change in pp
- `+lifecycle` … `+misc`, `total` — the reports a review batch filed, by kind
- safety audit columns — the Safety audit's metrics, as a landing changed them
- API stability columns — the landing's items by how `ffimap api` classifies their consumer-facing API against its base: `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed`, `new`, and `→Replaces` for the anchors a port moved; `unattributed` the crate's public items no anchor reaches, by module; `reasons` the changed and removed items with the reason the batch recorded
- `cost` / `review cost` / `total` — a module's translation, review and combined cost;
  `module wall` — first launch to final gate; `Σ recorded agents` leaves the assistant
  out, `Σ campaign` adds it, without per-unit cells
- `UB safe tests` … `Unit tests` — `#[test]` functions per suite, each with the coverage of
  running it alone; `Total tests` — all four, whose coverage is one joint run's union,
  never the sum
- `total`, `ported` and `wrapped` types and symbols — the scheduled public-API units, and
  those with a `Replaces:` or a `Wraps:` anchor at the tip; `share` is of the total

byte ranges, which a `unit_priv` test checks against C's literal; `utf8_charlen` is the
private `sequence_len(&[u8]) -> Option<usize>`; the three functions are the native
`decode_char(&[u8]) -> Result<(char, usize), InvalidCodePoint>`, `char_count(&[u8]) -> usize`
and `valid_prefix_len(&[u8]) -> usize`. What `git_utf8_iterate` accepts is always a scalar
value, so the code point is a `char`. One C defect is not carried over: with `str_len` 0,

no caller passes 0 (`next_hfs_char` loops while `*len`), and the port and its export refuse
empty bytes (-1, `*out` 0), documented on both and kept by a unit test. No out-of-tree
entity is used.

`ffi-export-src-util-utf8-c`, declared off in `Cargo.toml`: `git_utf8_iterate`,
`git_utf8_char_length` and `git_utf8_valid_buf_length`, under their C names, for
`path.c`'s `next_hfs_char`, `diff_xdiff.c`'s `git_xdiff_cb` and, on Windows, `fs_path.c`,
whose `port/unexport` stages are waves 232, 860 and 1531. Each body runs in ffibox's
`barrier`, a panic reported as -1 by `git_utf8_iterate` and aborting the two that cannot
fail, and each export is checked against its raw binding by a constant, `[sys::<name>,
<name>]`, whose function items coerce to one pointer type only where the signatures agree:
`str_len: u32` in an export fails to build (`E0308`). The three functions were allowlisted
(`wrapper.h` gains `utf8.h`) for that check and the equivalence tests. As a scratch check,
not a gate, the feature on links the exports in place of the archive's `utf8.o` (no
`utf8proc_utf8class` in the binary, C's `next_hfs_char` resolving to Rust): the six `equiv`
tests then compare the gateway with the native API and pass, and so do the tests of
`path.c` and `diff_xdiff.c`. The pointer findings of the four functions are submitted to
the ownership store.

content.content: --- name: ffibox description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one." --- # ffibox ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a value; what C does not alias is plain Rust. Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md` describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes. What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there. ## Planning ### Dependencies › Adopted crates A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists, each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses. ## Binding workflow ### Binding workflow › Rust tree The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory. ## Binding and porting Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`, `docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too. ### Binding types A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them. ### Binding types › Safe layout While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox;`, and `CArc` for `FooArc`. A value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal`. ### Binding symbols › Functions A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them. ### Binding symbols › Function pointers A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier, `callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body. A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a `CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as `docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table. ### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C. ### Porting › FFI boundary An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does with the Rust it reaches: - the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`, `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return its owners and handles; - memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C frees it through an exported release; - a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a `CPayload`; and - the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`. ### Porting types › Structs Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as [Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its `port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then the Rust ones. ---
name: ffimap
description: "Deterministic counts and sites of a Rust crate's unsafe and FFI surface. Read before a batch lands (its safe-boundary scan and safety-audit cells), when reviewing for unsafety, contracts or UB, and, as a hint only, when planning an audit's scope and worksets."
---

# ffimap

ffimap maps a Rust crate's FFI and unsafe surface deterministically: a rustc driver over
HIR and typeck counts unsafe blocks and fns, raw and void pointers by position and
visibility, FFI calls and wrapper use. No model is involved, so two runs over one tree
agree exactly. Its `--help` lists its flags, and its `docs/schema.md`, read in full before
its first scan, its counters and how a report combines them.

It counts what the build compiles of the safe crate itself, and prints one JSON document:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> > <file>.json
```

Every scan names the crate's seams, the functions that hand a value between its wrapper and
its raw form, so that each counter's `of_which.seam` share tells that plumbing apart from
the pointer management a consumer of the safe API faces: ffibox's handle seams `as_ptr`,
`as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr` and `from_void_ptr`, the ownership hand-offs
`from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`, the adoption of a raw C
value, `from_raw`, and the view of a C object as another, `as_object`. A crate built on
ffibox is scanned with `--ffibox`, and its `-sys` crates are named with `--sys-crates`:

```bash
ffimap <workdir> --ffibox --sys-crates <the -sys crates> --regions ffi_import,ffi_export \
    --seams as_ptr,as_mut_ptr,as_void_ptr,from_ptr,from_void_ptr,from_raw_parts,into_raw_parts,into_raw,from_c,into_c,as_c_ptr,from_raw,as_object \
    > <file>.json
```

Raw bindings that are a module of the crate, not a crate of their own, laid out and
generated as [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes, are named to `--sys-crates`
by their path, `crate::<path>`, beside the `-sys` crates that remain. A named module joins
the inventory and leaves every other counter, as a `-sys` crate does. Left unnamed, its C
types and functions are in no inventory, the cells that read it are taken over the other
crates' alone, and the generated code counts as the crate's own, all with no error. A module
that holds hand-written code beside its declarations is left unnamed, since naming it would
take that code out of the scan.

In a port campaign, a scan names with `--features` the export feature of every module not
yet switched, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Export features section
names them, so that the `ffi_export` gateways compiled under them are counted. Every scan
names the module's unsafe regions, as the conventions' Unsafe regions section names them,
with `--regions`.

Two scans are compared only when they name the same seams, regions and features.

Its counters form one tree, each named by its dotted path into the scan's `counts`, as
ffimap's `docs/schema.md` describes; a metric is a counter, or a combination of counters
that schema allows: a partition's leaves summed, a share read against the record it cuts,
or subtracted from it. `--sites <counter> ...` also lists where each named counter's
increments are, and takes leaves only, such as `fn.unsafe.pub`; the workspace is named
before it. The counters that recur:

- `fn.unsafe.pub`, the public `unsafe fn`s, the crate's public unsafe surface, of which
  `fn.unsafe.of_which.other.pub` are those neither a trait nor a seam required; and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, the raw pointers in
  their signatures;
- `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`, the
  raw pointers in public fields and in the signatures of public safe fns, together
  `raw_ptr.total.safe.pub`, the raw pointers on the safe public interface; and their
  `of_which.void` shares, the type-erased ones among them;
- `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, the references to a cell, less their
  `of_which.self_in_ref_accessor` and `of_which.self_in_trait_impl` shares, the positions
  ffibox sanctions: references to C memory where a handle belongs, which assert `noalias`,
  `readonly` or validity over memory C may write; `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std`, the same
  of the raw C structs; and `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`, the borrows,
  slices and strings formed from a raw pointer, over bytes C must neither free nor change
  while they live;
- `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`,
  each an unchecked assertion that a value may move to or be shared with another thread;
- `raw_ptr.deref.wr` and `raw_ptr.deref.rd`, raw-pointer writes and reads, each a pointer
  the implementer vouches is non-null, aligned, live, initialized and unaliased by a live
  reference; and
- `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}` and
  `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`, the types that hold a raw pointer and
  tear it down or copy it by hand, and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.none.{pub,priv}`, those
  that declare nothing about it. Each of these five also has a `.total`, the sum of its two
  leaves, which is no leaf for `--sites`.

ffimap is neither complete nor sound: its sites are where review starts, not all it
covers. It does not count the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, such as a reference
or lifetime-annotated handle made from a raw pointer by `&*p`, `from_ptr`, `from_raw` or
`from_raw_parts`, or changed by a `transmute`: those are found in the source.

What follows is how ffimap serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffimap adds there.

## Binding and porting

### Binding › Safe boundary

Before a batch lands, a scan with `--sites fn.unsafe.pub raw_ptr.field.pub
raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub` lists the public
`unsafe fn`s and the raw pointers on the safe public interface, and each of those sites
that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed.
Its `--sites` also name the unsafe code outside both regions,
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.outside_regions`, another crate's macro expansions included,
which the `unsafe_code` lint misses, and `fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions.pub` and
`.priv`: outside the raw bindings, each of those sites in the batch's changeset is moved
into its region.

## Accounting

### Accounting › Landing cells

A batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: safety audit` table is the change in each of
the Safety audit's metrics, from a scan of the tip its landing rebased onto to a scan of
the tree it lands.

### Accounting › API stability

`ffimap api` measures a safe crate's consumer-facing API per C item, from rustdoc JSON, as
its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the
`<kind>::<path>` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor
names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract
[`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer:
the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer
can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc
JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose
`format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of
the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

## Reviewing

---
name: wavefront
description: "Deterministic queries and dependency-ordered plans over the C codebase, the first resort for any question about it: entities, uses, dependencies, pointers, lifecycles, T3 cast tables. Read before querying the C codebase, before planning, decomposing or scheduling, before analysing or binding an item, when packing wrap batches, when reviewing pointer findings or lifecycles, and before changing wavefront itself."
---

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits

# wavefront

dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.
